analysis|01-01|-45|Τίθεται σε ισχύ το Ιουλιανό ημερολόγιο|The Julian calendar takes effect|The Roman calendar of the time was largely unconnected to the solar year. The months followed the phases of the Moon, and the priesthoods added extra months whenever they judged it fit, so the seasons gradually shifted. Julius Caesar, as a powerful politician and chief priest, sought a radical reform and consulted the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes, who knew the length of the solar year better. This change became known as the Julian reform and marked a new era in the measurement of time. // The new calendar was based on a year of 365 days, with one extra day every four years. To align the chronology with the seasons, the year 46 BC lasted unusually long, and for that reason it remained known as the year of confusion. The new reckoning began to apply on 1 January 45 BC, and the calendar took Caesar's name. It was soon applied across the whole Roman territory. In this way the dates of festivals and the seasons were stabilised for many centuries. // The Julian calendar remained in use in Europe for about sixteen centuries, until the more accurate Gregorian calendar was introduced in 1582. Adding one day every four years was not perfectly accurate, and the deviation accumulated over time. Even today some Orthodox churches use the Julian calendar for their ecclesiastical life. This reform is one of the most lasting legacies of the Roman era. The length of the year it used was quite close to the real one, which is remarkable for the time.

analysis|01-01|1801|Ο Πιάτσι ανακαλύπτει την Δήμητρα|Piazzi discovers Ceres|In the nineteenth century astronomers assumed that an unknown body lay between Mars and Jupiter, since the spacing of the orbits seemed to leave a gap. Giuseppe Piazzi, director of the Palermo observatory, systematically recording the positions of the stars, noticed a moving object. The discovery came at a time when astronomy was rapidly becoming systematic, with new telescopes and star catalogues. // At first he considered it a comet, but its motion proved steadier and matched a path among the planets. Piazzi fell ill and for a time lost sight of the object. It was found again months later, thanks to the calculations of Gauss, which gave the body's course across the sky. The objects of the asteroid belt are studied today with space missions, and Ceres has been visited by the Dawn spacecraft. // Ceres, as it was named, was the first of the objects we now call asteroids. In its early years it was regarded as a planet, until other similar bodies were found in the same region. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union classified it as a dwarf planet. The discovery opened the way to the study of the asteroid belt and to a new classification of the Solar System. The old designation as a planet still draws interest, because the object remains a point of reference for scientists.

analysis|01-01|1804|Η Αϊτή γίνεται ανεξάρτητη|Haiti becomes independent|The colony of Saint-Domingue was the most profitable French possession in the Caribbean, with an economy based on sugar cultivation and slavery. The French Revolution of 1789 brought ideas of liberty, which were not applied immediately to the enslaved. In 1791 a great slave uprising broke out, which developed into a long revolutionary conflict. // During the struggle, leaders such as Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines fought French, British and Spanish forces. France abolished slavery in 1794, but Napoleon later tried to restore it with an expedition that proved unsuccessful. On 1 January 1804 Dessalines proclaimed independence, and the new state took the indigenous name Haiti. The history of Haiti is often cited as an example of the clash between freedom and the economic interests of colonialism. // The independence of Haiti was unique, because it was won by people who had been enslaved and who overturned a colonial system. The new state faced for decades international isolation and economic pressure, as the great powers hesitated to recognise it. Recognition came late and with heavy financial conditions, which affected the country for decades. Today the anniversary recalls the struggle of people who lived under a regime of slavery.

analysis|01-01|1863|Η Διακήρυξη Χειραφέτησης του Λίνκολν|Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation|The American Civil War broke out when Southern states left the Union, chiefly in order to secure slavery. President Lincoln, without initially making its abolition his aim, changed course as the war demanded new goals. After the important military development at Antietam in 1862, he prepared a text that he would issue at the right moment. // On 1 January 1863 he signed the Proclamation, which declared that enslaved people in the states in rebellion were free. The act did not cover the states that remained in the Union, nor the areas that were already under Union army control. Nevertheless it opened the way for the enlistment of Black soldiers in the Union army, which changed the course of the war. Thousands of Black Americans served in the Union army and contributed significantly to the outcome of the war. // The Proclamation gave the conflict a moral meaning and strengthened the decision to abolish slavery throughout the country. The Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution, ratified in 1865, abolished it definitively. Full equality of citizens, however, required decades of struggle after the Proclamation. Lincoln's act remains one of the central milestones of American history and of the struggle for human rights.

analysis|01-01|1899|Τελειώνει η ισπανική κυριαρχία στην Κούβα|Spanish rule in Cuba ends|Cuba had spent decades struggling for independence from Spain, with great uprisings in 1868 and 1895. The United States, which had economic interests on the island, intervened in this struggle after the incident with the cruiser Maine in Havana. The Spanish-American War of 1898 resulted in the defeat of Spain. // Under the treaty that followed, Spain acknowledged the loss of its colonies in the region and withdrew from the island. On 1 January 1899 power passed to the American occupying forces, and Cuba was placed under military administration. The Cuban fighters, who had fought for years, thus found themselves in a new and uncertain situation. The Spanish empire in the New World had now lost most of its colonies. // The American occupation lasted until 1902, when Cuba acquired its own constitutional republic. Nevertheless, the new relationship with the United States, which included special terms for intervention, deeply affected the political life of the island for decades. Cuba gained its nominal independence in 1902, but the terms of its relationship with the United States continued to be debated.

analysis|01-01|1947|Οι Καναδοί αποκτούν δική τους ιθαγένεια|Canadians gain their own citizenship|Until the mid-twentieth century, the inhabitants of Canada were considered British subjects, because Canada was an autonomous state within the Commonwealth, with the British crown as the common symbol. As the country gained ever greater autonomy, the need for its own legal status became pressing. After the Second World War the government legislated a distinct citizenship. // The new law came into force on 1 January 1947, and from that moment Canadians who were born or had rights in the country acquired Canadian citizenship. British subjects living in the country were converted into citizens of Canada through a specific legal procedure. The change was symbolic but also practical, because it defined who belongs to the state. This citizenship provided a common legal framework in a country with a strong French-speaking and English-speaking identity. // The acquisition of its own citizenship became a milestone in the national identity of Canada. The country thus acquired a clearer and distinct legal framework, while the bond with Britain remained at the level of the Commonwealth. This legislation is considered today fundamental to the development of the Canadian state under the rule of law. Canada has maintained its link with the British crown through the Commonwealth, which remains the case today.

analysis|01-01|1959|Ο Μπατίστα εγκαταλείπει την Κούβα|Batista leaves Cuba|Fulgencio Batista had come to power through a coup in 1952 and governed Cuba by authoritarian means, in a country marked by sharp social inequalities and corruption. Fidel Castro, by contrast, with the 26th of July Movement, was fighting from the mountains of the Sierra Maestra. The rebels gradually gained ground, as opposition to the regime grew. Corruption and the repression of the regime had alienated a large part of the population of the capital. // On 1 January 1959 Batista left the island, and his forces quickly disintegrated. Castro's revolution took control of power, without meeting substantial resistance in the cities. The moment is considered the beginning of a new era for the island. Castro had initially sought to lead a broader movement, with the aim of democratic change. // The new government carried out radical reforms, with nationalisations and land redistribution, which provoked fierce conflicts with the United States. In 1961 relations were broken off, while Cuba drew closer to the Soviet Union. The revolution thus became a central event of the Cold War in the Western Hemisphere. The period that followed changed Cuba's geopolitical position and made it an ally of the Soviet Union.

analysis|01-01|1999|Το ευρώ μπαίνει σε κυκλοφορία ως λογιστικό νόμισμα|The euro enters circulation as an accounting currency|The European Union had prepared for a common currency through the Maastricht Treaty of 1992, which set convergence criteria for the member states. The idea was to reduce transaction costs and strengthen the economic integration of the continent. The negotiations were long and difficult, since each country had different economic structures. // On 1 January 1999 the euro was introduced as an accounting currency, for markets and banks, in eleven countries. The national currencies remained in circulation, while euro prices were calculated at fixed exchange rates. Greece did not take part at that moment, as it did not yet meet the criteria, while Denmark, Sweden and the United Kingdom chose to stay out. The new currency limited the risk of exchange rate fluctuations between the participating countries. // The introduction of the euro was a historic step towards the monetary unification of Europe. The common monetary policy was assigned to the European Central Bank, which began to operate as an autonomous institution. This course strongly affected the economies of the countries and opened discussions about the stability of the eurozone. Greece took part later, in 2001, and the process showed how demanding adjustment to the criteria was.

analysis|01-02|1492|Παραδίδεται η Γρανάδα|Granada surrenders|The Iberian Peninsula experienced centuries of successive conflicts between the Christian kingdoms and the Muslim states. The last Muslim kingdom in the region was the Emirate of Granada, which had survived for centuries through alliances and retreats. The unification of the Christian kingdoms of Castile and Aragon put considerable pressure on the emirate. For centuries Granada was a centre of culture and architecture, with the Alhambra as the symbol of the era. // The war for the capture of the city lasted several months, with siege and fierce battles. Finally, the last emir, known as Boabdil, handed the city over to the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, in early January 1492. The surrender marked the end of the Reconquista, the long effort of the Christians to reconquer the Iberian Peninsula. The terms of the surrender included guarantees for the religious and property rights of the inhabitants, which were not always respected. // The capture of Granada profoundly changed the political balance of Spain. A few months later, the Alhambra Decree forced the Jews of Spain to be exiled or baptised. In the same year, the Spanish throne turned towards wider maritime exploration, with the voyage of Columbus as the best-known example. This date is considered a milestone of European history, because it is linked to the beginning of the great voyages of maritime exploration.

analysis|01-02|1942|Οι Ιάπωνες καταλαμβάνουν τη Μανίλα|Japanese take Manila|The Philippines was an American possession when Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Japan aimed to secure raw materials and to create a broad sphere of control in Asia and the Pacific. The American and Filipino troops were in an inferior position, without adequate air cover. // Japanese troops entered Manila on 2 January 1942, and the capital of the Philippines fell relatively quickly. The American and Filipino forces withdrew to fortified positions, such as the Bataan peninsula and the island of Corregidor. The defence there lasted for months, while the inhabitants suffered from hunger and repression. The capture of Manila was part of Japan's rapid advance into South-East Asia in early 1942. // The occupation that followed lasted until 1945, when the Allies liberated the Philippines. The experience left deep marks on society, with heavy civilian losses and destruction of infrastructure. The war in the Philippines thus became one of the harshest chapters of the Asian theatre of the Second World War. The city had already suffered bombing, and the American forces had withdrawn before the Japanese arrived. The occupation was linked to violent acts against the inhabitants, which remain in history as a dark chapter.

analysis|01-02|1959|Εκτοξεύεται το Luna 1|Luna 1 is launched|After the launch of Sputnik in 1957, the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union for space supremacy was intense. The Soviet Union aimed to reach the Moon first, and the Luna programme was part of this effort. The first craft of the series were tested with varying success. // Luna 1 was launched on 2 January 1959 and was the first human-made object to escape Earth's gravity. It passed close to the Moon and then entered orbit around the Sun, something unprecedented at the time. The mission, although it did not reach the Moon in terms of a landing, recorded significant data on the space environment. // The success of Luna 1 was an important step for research space technology. The mission opened the way for the next craft of the series, which later succeeded in photographing the far side of the Moon. The achievement confirmed the capabilities of the Soviet space industry at that time. The mission was built with limited means, but it showed the ability of the Soviet Union to send craft beyond the Earth. The mission contributed to modern astronomy and opened the way for the following missions to the Moon.

analysis|01-02|1967|Ο Ρόναλντ Ρίγκαν ορκίζεται κυβερνήτης της Καλιφόρνιας|Ronald Reagan is sworn in as governor of California|Ronald Reagan was a Hollywood actor before becoming involved in politics, first as a member of the Democratic Party and later as a Republican. His presence in public life grew in the early 1960s, when he supported conservative positions. California was then the state with the largest economy in the United States, and many political forces watched it with particular attention. // In early January 1967 Reagan took office as governor of the state, having won the elections of 1966. His term was marked by tax cuts, strengthening of the police and confrontation with student movements. This experience gave him executive experience, which he later put to use in national elections. Among his political positions were the reduction of taxation and limited state intervention in the economy. // The governorship of Reagan was the starting point of his political career. In 1980 he was elected President of the United States, and his policy strongly influenced the 1980s and the philosophy of conservatism. His path demonstrates the importance of local power as a proving ground for wider national leadership. His course became an example for many politicians, who later followed a similar route from state office.

analysis|01-02|1974|Όριο ταχύτητας 55 μιλίων στους αμερικανικούς δρόμους|55 mph speed limit on American roads|During the 1970s the world oil market was hit by an embargo imposed by members of OPEC, after the Yom Kippur War. Prices soared and the United States faced fuel shortages and queues at the petrol stations. The government sought ways to save energy in every sector. // President Nixon signed the law that set a maximum speed limit of 55 miles per hour on American motorways, with the aim of reducing fuel consumption. The measure concerned almost all the states and was widely applied. The decision marked state intervention in the everyday life of drivers. The measure was part of a wider energy policy package that sought to limit dependence on imported crude oil. // This rule remained in force for several years and became a symbol of the energy crisis of the era. The consequences of the embargo led both to the development of alternative energy sources and to an increase in the efficiency of cars. The limit was later abolished, but it remained a characteristic intervention in a period of crisis. Petrol stations had extensive queues at the end of 1973, and the situation pushed the government into immediate decisions. The restriction was eventually relaxed and abolished in the 1990s, when market conditions had changed.

analysis|01-02|2008|Το πετρέλαιο φτάνει τα 100 δολάρια το βαρέλι|Oil reaches 100 dollars a barrel|In the early years of the 21st century, global energy demand rose, mainly because of the rapid industrial development of China and India. Production did not keep pace with demand, and the market was sensitive to geopolitical developments. At the same time, the value of the dollar was low, which favoured commodity prices. // On 2 January 2008 the price of crude oil exceeded 100 dollars a barrel for the first time. The rise was linked to speculative investments and to the perception that reserves were limited. The media highlighted the event as a turning point for the world economy. The rise in prices was connected with intense demand from emerging economies and with the reduction of stocks. // This record did not last as a stable price, since oil rose even further during 2008. However, the economic crisis that followed led to a sharp fall in prices. The event showed how vulnerable the world economy is to fluctuations in the energy market. Several analysts also examined the role of speculation in tradeable raw materials. This extreme price showed how sensitive the world economy is to fluctuations in oil.

analysis|01-03|1521|Ο πάπας αφορίζει τον Λούθηρο|The pope excommunicates Luther|In the sixteenth century the Church of Rome was deeply involved in matters of power and financing, while the sale of indulgences provoked intense indignation. Martin Luther, a professor of theology at Wittenberg, published in 1517 his Ninety-Five Theses, which criticised this practice and called for theological debate. The dispute escalated quickly, with public lectures and written replies. The spread of printed texts allowed his positions to circulate rapidly throughout Europe. // The bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, issued by Pope Leo X in early 1521, was the official decision to excommunicate Luther. With it Luther was excluded from the Catholic Church, while Emperor Charles V summoned him to the Diet of Worms. Luther refused to retract his positions and continued his work under the protection of princes who supported him. The excommunication also had a legal dimension, since it removed from Luther the protection of the legal system of the time. // The excommunication did not stop the Reformation, but made it irreversible. The split of Western Christianity led to the creation of the Protestant Churches, which differed from Catholic teaching and the structure of authority. The conflict left deep marks on politics, religious life and the intellectual life of Europe for centuries. The Reformation also influenced art, music and education, with long-lasting consequences.

analysis|01-03|1777|Ο Τζορτζ Ουάσινγκτον νικά τους Βρετανούς στο Πρίνστον|George Washington defeats the British at Princeton|At the end of 1776 the American army was in a difficult position. Washington's forces had retreated from much of New York and New Jersey, while many soldiers were leaving as their terms of service ended. The victory at Trenton, shortly before Christmas, gave a breathing space, but the situation remained unstable. // On 3 January 1777 Washington attacked British forces near Princeton in New Jersey and defeated them. The battle was brief but decisive, and the British were forced to rearrange their positions in the area. The American army gained a valuable advantage without losing its basic strength. The experience of the winter strengthened the cohesion of the army, which was decisive for what followed. // The victory raised the morale of the revolutionaries during the difficult winter period. The army spent the winter in safer positions, while the experience helped improve its organisation. Many historians regard Princeton as a turning point that strengthened the resilience of the Americans during the War of Independence. Washington used the victory to keep the army together during a difficult phase of the war.

analysis|01-03|1833|Το Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο παίρνει τα νησιά Φώκλαντ|The United Kingdom takes the Falkland Islands|The Falklands lie in the South Atlantic and were claimed by various European powers over the centuries of navigation. After the independence of the Latin American countries, the newly founded Argentina claimed their sovereignty as a continuation of Spanish rights. It had even established a small settlement there in the 1820s. The islands occupy a strategic position, close to the shipping routes of the South Atlantic. // In January 1833 British forces landed on the islands, and the Argentine authorities were forced to withdraw. The British restored colonial administration and then encouraged the settlement of British colonists. This move became the starting point of the long-running dispute over sovereignty. The dispute has been discussed in international organisations, without a definitive solution. // The dispute remained open for a long historical period, and in 1982 it led to war between the United Kingdom and Argentina. Argentina continues to claim the islands to this day, while their inhabitants, in a referendum, have chosen to remain a British territory. The question continues to affect relations between the two countries. The war of 1982 remains in history as a major conflict, which affected the lives of both countries.

analysis|01-03|1959|Η Αλάσκα γίνεται πολιτεία των ΗΠΑ|Alaska becomes a US state|Alaska had been bought from Russia in 1867 and for decades remained an American territory without full political rights. Its inhabitants had long sought admission as a state, while its supporters held that its vast area and strategic role justified it. In 1958 the law preparing its admission was approved. Alaska is the largest US state by area and has rich natural resources. // In early January 1959 the 49th state of the United States was officially proclaimed. Alaska became the largest state by area, with varied natural landscapes and a sparse population. Its admission came a few months before that of Hawaii, which became the 50th state. Its acquisition from Russia was initially criticised as a useless transaction, but it proved strategically significant. // The admission of Alaska opened the way to its economic development, mainly through the discovery of large oil deposits shortly afterwards. The transport of oil to the south became a key pillar of the local economy. The moment is regarded as a milestone for the territorial unity of the United States. Today the state is an area of activity in energy, fishing and tourism.

analysis|01-03|1977|Ιδρύεται η Apple Computer|Apple Computer is founded|In the mid-1970s personal computers were still rare and addressed to a few technology enthusiasts. In California, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak had built the first small computer board, with their interest focused on the hobbyist world. The two men wanted to turn their idea into a business, and so they sought funding and help. The establishment of personal computers was linked to new ideas about the everyday use of technology. // The company was officially registered in early January 1977, with the participation of Mike Markkula, an investor with experience in technology. Markkula brought organisation and capital, which made possible the commercial production of the Apple II. The small organisation quickly became known among technology enthusiasts. The company started with a small capital, but the success of the Apple II gave impetus to its growth. // The creation of Apple was decisive for the spread of the personal computer into homes and schools. The company contributed to shaping computers with graphical interfaces and the mouse, ideas that later appeared in the Macintosh. Today Apple is one of the largest technology companies in the world. The founding of Apple symbolises the passage from the amateur garage to an industry of worldwide reach.

analysis|01-04|1884|Ιδρύεται η Εταιρεία των Φαβιανών|The Fabian Society is founded|At the end of the nineteenth century British society experienced sharp inequalities, and socialist ideas were gaining ground among intellectuals. The Industrial Revolution had created large urban masses of workers in conditions of poverty. In this climate, a circle of educated people sought a reformist alternative to revolutionary solutions. // On 4 January 1884 the Fabian Society was founded in London, with members such as Sidney and Beatrice Webb and George Bernard Shaw. The group argued that socialism should be achieved gradually, through legislative and educational reforms, not through revolution. The members organised lectures, studies and publications to promote their ideas. The Fabian movement took its name from the Roman general Fabius, who had preferred the gradual tactic. // The Society exerted considerable influence on the British Labour Party, which took shape in the early twentieth century, and on the design of the welfare state. The approach of gradual reform became central to the British social democratic tradition. The influence of the Fabians also appeared in the political thought of many other countries. The group attracted educated people and politicians with a broad range of ideas, from social reformers to writers.

analysis|01-04|1896|Η Γιούτα γίνεται η 45η πολιτεία|Utah becomes the 45th state|The territory of Utah had come under the United States after the war with Mexico, and was inhabited mainly by Mormons. The religious community had adopted polygamy, which was incompatible with American legal conceptions. Congress refused for years to admit the territory, until the community agreed to give up polygamy. Admission came considerably later than for other western territories, since the process lasted decades. // President Grover Cleveland signed the proclamation of admission on 4 January 1896, and Utah became the 45th state. The admission sealed a long process of compromise between the religious tradition and federal requirements. The state constitution included an explicit prohibition of polygamy. The state authorities adopted a constitution that included educational and political guarantees. // Utah's entry into the Union allowed it to take equal part in federal politics. The state has since developed a distinctive social and economic identity, with a strong influence from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The case is an example of the conflict between religious practices and state rules in American history. Admission is analysed today as an example of combining religious identity with institutional compliance.

analysis|01-04|1948|Η Βιρμανία γίνεται ανεξάρτητη|Burma becomes independent|Burma had been a British colony since the middle of the nineteenth century. During the Second World War Japan had occupied it, and the nationalists who resisted cooperated with the British only temporarily. Aung San, the principal leader of the nationalist movement, negotiated independence, but he was assassinated in 1947, before the process was completed. The colonial period left deep marks on the economy and administration of the country, with limited education for the majority. // On 4 January 1948 the country officially gained its independence, with U Nu as its first prime minister. The new state faced at the same time civil wars and armed uprisings by ethnic groups and communist movements. Democratic governance did not last long, as the army seized power in 1962. In 1947 the Panglong Agreement was concluded, which laid the foundations for independence. // The independence of Burma was part of the wave of decolonisation in Asia after the war. The country, which since 1989 has been called Myanmar, still lives with the consequences of internal conflicts and military regimes. The history of its independence remains central to understanding the country's present politics. The date is today a national holiday and recalls the long effort for self-government.

analysis|01-04|2010|Εγκαινιάζεται ο Μπουρτζ Χαλίφα|The Burj Khalifa is inaugurated|At the beginning of the twenty-first century Dubai experienced very rapid economic growth, based on tourism, property and services. The city's authorities wished to raise its profile on the world map with striking architectural projects. The skyscraper was designed with the aim of becoming the tallest building in the world. The construction was part of a wider programme of architectural and tourist projects in the city. // The Burj Khalifa was inaugurated in January 2010 and, at a height of 828 metres, became the tallest skyscraper in the world. Its construction required complex engineering, with special foundations and systems for dealing with wind and heat. The inauguration ceremony attracted the attention of the media across the world. The skyscraper is named in honour of the ruler of the country, Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan. // The building strengthened Dubai's image as a city with ambitious architecture and a strong commercial life. Its success also influenced the planning of other skyscrapers in the area. Despite doubts about its cost and sustainability, the skyscraper remains a symbol of the urban ambition of the era. The Burj Khalifa has an observation deck at great height and is a magnet for tourists from all over the world.

analysis|01-05|1875|Εγκαινιάζεται το Παλέ Γκαρνιέ στο Παρίσι|The Palais Garnier is inaugurated in Paris|In the nineteenth century Paris was being transformed by major infrastructure projects, under the direction of Georges-Eugène Haussmann. Emperor Napoleon III wished for a magnificent opera house that would reflect the prestige of the regime. The competition announced in 1861 was won by the young architect Charles Garnier. The building was one of the largest theatrical works of its time, with an impressive ensemble of marble and decoration. // Construction lasted for years, with interruptions caused by political upheavals and the war. The building was inaugurated in January 1875 with a splendid ceremony and the presence of high society. Its rich decoration and magnificent space were admired by contemporaries. Its staircase and great hall became models for many other opera buildings around the world. // The Palais Garnier became a symbol of the cultural life of Paris and one of the best-known buildings in Europe. Its history inspired literature too, the best-known example being the novel The Phantom of the Opera. The building continues to host performances and to attract visitors from all over the world. Today it houses performances of the Paris National Opera and is a popular attraction.

analysis|01-05|1925|Η πρώτη γυναίκα κυβερνήτης στις ΗΠΑ|The first woman governor in the US|Women's suffrage in the United States was secured by the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, after decades of struggle by the suffragists. However, the participation of women in the executive power was rare. Wyoming had recognised women's right to vote as early as the nineteenth century, which is why it was regarded as a pioneer. Women's suffrage was recognised constitutionally, and her election strengthened the argument for equal participation in politics. // Nellie Tayloe Ross was elected governor of the state and took up her duties on 5 January 1925, as successor to her husband, who had died. Her election was historic, as she was the first woman to govern a US state. Her term focused on questions of social welfare and state administration. She herself distinguished herself through her administration and the energy with which she defended the interests of the state. // Her election opened the way for other women in the political life of the United States. She later served as director of the United States Mint, a position that was also unusual for a woman of that era. Her story is a point of reference for the participation of women in public administration. The era opened the way for many women who sought political roles at national level.

analysis|01-05|1933|Ξεκινά η κατασκευή της Γέφυρας του Χρυσού Πύλης|Construction of the Golden Gate Bridge begins|San Francisco lies on a peninsula, and for decades the connection with the northern shore was made by ferry. As the city grew, the need for a permanent road link became pressing. The engineers faced great challenges, because of the strong currents, the fog and the depth of the strait. The name of the bridge is linked to the strait that separates the bay of San Francisco from the Pacific. // Construction of the bridge began in early January 1933, during the period of the Great Depression. The idea had been promoted by the engineer Joseph Strauss, while the design of the arches was assigned to other engineers. The project required large investments and hard work, and several workers lost their lives during its course. The bridge opened to traffic in 1937 and is known for the fog that often covers the strait. // The bridge was inaugurated in 1937 and immediately became a symbol of the city. Its orange-red colour and distinctive silhouette made it one of the most recognisable structures in the United States. The work proved a model for the engineering of large bridges and remains an important site of American culture. The project was a landmark of engineering and is still today one of the most photographed monuments in the United States.

analysis|01-05|1968|Ο Ντούμπτσεκ ηγέτης του Κομμουνιστικού Κόμματος|Dubček becomes leader of the Communist Party|After the Second World War Czechoslovakia was a state in the Soviet sphere of influence, with an authoritarian regime and persistent economic problems. The hard-line leadership of Antonín Novotný found it difficult to meet demands for reform, particularly from intellectuals and young people. Tension with Moscow was intense, while Slovakia demanded greater autonomy. Czechoslovakia had a long history of national conflicts between Czechs and Slovaks, which affected the form of the state. // In early January 1968 the Central Committee of the party elected Alexander Dubček as First Secretary, in place of Novotný. Dubček launched a programme of liberalisation, known as "socialism with a human face", with greater freedom of the press, relaxed censorship and more rights for organisations. This period came to be called the Prague Spring. The reform of the economy and freedom of speech were demands that other societies of the region later also expressed. // Moscow considered that the reforms threatened the unity of the Soviet bloc. In August 1968 troops of the Warsaw Pact invaded the country and abruptly ended the experiment. Dubček was removed from power the following year, and a period of political conformity and purges followed. The Prague Spring remained a symbol of the desire for freedom, and in 1989 the changes in Europe brought the city back to the forefront.

analysis|01-06|1066|Ο Χάρολντ Γκόντγουινσον στέφεται βασιλιάς της Αγγλίας|Harold Godwinson is crowned king of England|In eleventh-century England the succession to the throne was disputed. King Edward the Confessor left no direct heir, and several people put forward claims. Harold Godwinson, a powerful earl of Wessex and counsellor of the king, had the support of the English nobles.
